{{Short description|Study of dimension in algebraic geometry}}
In [[mathematics]], '''dimension theory''' is the study in terms of [[commutative algebra]] of the notion of [[dimension of an algebraic variety]] (and by extension that of a [[Scheme (mathematics)|scheme]]). The need of a ''theory'' for such an apparently simple notion results from the existence of many definitions of dimension that are equivalent only in the most regular cases (see [[Dimension of an algebraic variety]]). A large part of dimension theory consists in studying the conditions under which several dimensions are equal, and many important classes of [[commutative ring]]s may be defined as the rings such that two dimensions are equal; for example, a [[regular ring]] is a commutative ring such that the [[global dimension|homological dimension]] is equal to the [[Krull dimension]].

The theory is simpler for [[commutative ring]]s that are [[finitely generated algebra]]s over a field, which are also [[quotient ring]]s of [[polynomial ring]]s in a finite number of indeterminates over a field. In this case, which is the algebraic counterpart of the case of [[affine algebraic set]]s, most of the definitions of the dimension are equivalent. For general commutative rings, the lack of geometric interpretation is an obstacle to the development of the theory; in particular, very little is known for non-[[Noetherian ring|Noetherian rings]]. (Kaplansky's ''Commutative rings'' gives a good account of the non-Noetherian case.)

Throughout the article, <math>\dim</math> denotes [[Krull dimension]] of a ring and <math>\operatorname{ht}</math> the [[height (ring theory)|height]] of a [[prime ideal]] (i.e., the Krull dimension of the [[Localization (commutative algebra)|localization]] at that prime ideal). Rings are assumed to be commutative except in the last section on dimensions of non-commutative rings.

== Basic results ==

Let <math>R</math> be a [[Noetherian ring]] or a [[valuation ring]]. Then
<math display="block">\dim R[x] = \dim R + 1.</math>
If <math>R</math> is noetherian, this follows from the fundamental theorem below (in particular, [[Krull's principal ideal theorem]]), but it is also a consequence of a more precise result. For any prime ideal <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> in <math>R</math>,
<math display="block">\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak{p} R[x]) = \operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak{p}).</math>
<math display="block">\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak{q}) = \operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak{p}) + 1</math> for any prime ideal <math>\mathfrak{q} \supsetneq \mathfrak{p} R[x]</math> in <math>R[x]</math> that contracts to <math>\mathfrak{p}</math>.
This can be shown within basic ring theory (cf. Kaplansky, commutative rings). In addition, in each fiber of <math>\operatorname{Spec} R[x] \to \operatorname{Spec} R</math>, one cannot have a chain of primes ideals of length <math>\ge 2</math>.

Since an [[Artinian ring]] (e.g., a field) has dimension zero, by induction one gets a formula: for an artinian ring <math>R</math>,
<math display="block">\dim R[x_1, \dots, x_n] = n.</math>

== Local rings ==

=== Fundamental theorem ===
Let <math>(R, \mathfrak{m})</math> be a Noetherian [[local ring]] and <math>I</math> a <math>\mathfrak{m}</math>-[[primary ideal]] (i.e., it sits between some power of <math>\mathfrak{m}</math> and <math>\mathfrak{m}</math>). Let <math>F(t)</math> be the [[Hilbert–Poincaré series|Poincaré series]] of the [[associated graded ring]] <math display="inline">\operatorname{gr}_I R = \bigoplus_0^\infty I^n / I^{n+1}</math>. That is,
<math display="block">F(t) = \sum_0^\infty \ell(I^n / I^{n+1}) t^n</math>
where <math>\ell</math> refers to the [[length of a module]] (over an Artinian ring <math>(\operatorname{gr}_I R)_0 = R/I</math>). If <math>x_1, \dots, x_s</math> generate <math>I</math>, then their image in <math>I/I^2</math> have degree 1 and generate <math>\operatorname{gr}_I R</math> as <math>R/I</math>-algebra. By the [[Hilbert–Serre theorem]], <math>F</math> is a [[rational function]] with exactly one pole at <math>t=1</math> of order <math>d \le s</math>. Since
<math display="block">(1-t)^{-d} = \sum_0^\infty \binom{d-1+j}{d-1} t^j,</math>
we find that the coefficient of <math>t^n</math> in <math>F(t) = (1-t)^d F(t) (1 - t)^{-d}</math> is of the form
<math display="block">\sum_0^N a_k \binom{d-1+n - k}{d-1} = (1 - t)^d F(t)\big|_{t=1} {n^{d-1} \over {d-1}!} + O(n^{d-2}).</math>
That is to say, <math>\ell(I^n / I^{n+1})</math> is a polynomial <math>P</math> in <math>n</math> of degree <math>d - 1</math>. <math>P</math> is called the [[Hilbert polynomial]] of <math>\operatorname{gr}_I R</math>.

We set <math>d(R) = d</math>. We also set <math>\delta(R)</math> to be the minimum number of elements of <math>R</math> that can generate an <math>\mathfrak{m}</math>-primary ideal of <math>R</math>. Our ambition is to prove the '''fundamental theorem''':
<math display="block">\delta(R) = d(R) = \dim R.</math>
Since we can take <math>s</math> to be <math>\delta(R)</math>, we already have <math>\delta(R) \ge d(R)</math> from the above. Next we prove <math>d(R) \ge \dim R</math> by induction on <math>d(R)</math>. Let <math>\mathfrak{p}_0 \subsetneq \cdots \subsetneq \mathfrak{p}_m</math> be a chain of prime ideals in <math>R</math>. Let <math>D = R/\mathfrak{p}_0</math> and <math>x</math> a nonzero nonunit element in <math>D</math>. Since <math>x</math> is not a zero-divisor, we have the exact sequence
<math display="block">0 \to D \overset{x}\to D \to D/xD \to 0.</math>
The degree bound of the Hilbert-Samuel polynomial now implies that <math>d(D) > d(D/xD) \ge d(R/\mathfrak{p}_1)</math>. (This essentially follows from the [[Artin–Rees lemma]]; see [[Hilbert–Samuel function]] for the statement and the proof.) In <math>R/\mathfrak{p}_1</math>, the chain <math>\mathfrak{p}_i</math> becomes a chain of length <math>m - 1</math> and so, by inductive hypothesis and again by the degree estimate,
<math display="block">m-1 \le \dim (R/\mathfrak{p}_1) \le d(R/\mathfrak{p}_1) \le d(D) - 1 \le d(R) - 1.</math>
The claim follows. It now remains to show <math>\dim R \ge \delta(R).</math> More precisely, we shall show:
{{math theorem|name=Lemma|math_statement= The maximal ideal <math>\mathfrak{m}</math> contains elements <math>x_1, \dots, x_d</math>, <math>d</math> = Krull dimension of <math>R</math>, such that, for any <math>i</math>, any prime ideal containing <math>(x_1, \dots, x_i)</math> has height&nbsp;<math>\ge i</math>.}}
(Notice: <math>(x_1, \dots, x_d)</math> is then <math>\mathfrak{m}</math>-primary.) The proof is omitted. It appears, for example, in Atiyah–MacDonald. But it can also be supplied privately; the idea is to use [[prime avoidance]].

=== Consequences of the fundamental theorem ===
Let <math>(R, \mathfrak{m})</math> be a noetherian local ring and put <math>k = R/\mathfrak{m}</math>. Then
*<math>\dim R \le \dim_k \mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2</math>, since a basis of <math>\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2</math> lifts to a generating set of <math>\mathfrak{m}</math> by Nakayama. If the equality holds, then <math>R</math> is called a [[regular local ring]].
*<math>\dim \widehat{R} = \dim R</math>, since <math>\operatorname{gr}R = \operatorname{gr}\widehat{R}</math>.
*([[Krull's principal ideal theorem]]) The height of the ideal generated by elements <math>x_1, \dots, x_s</math> in a Noetherian ring is at most <math>s</math>. Conversely, a prime ideal of height <math>s</math> is [[minimal prime ideal|minimal]] over an ideal generated by <math>s</math> elements. (Proof: Let <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> be a prime ideal minimal over such an ideal. Then <math>s \ge \dim R_\mathfrak{p} = \operatorname{ht} \mathfrak{p}</math>. The converse was shown in the course of the proof of the fundamental theorem.)

{{math_theorem|If <math>A \to B</math> is a morphism of noetherian local rings, then<ref>{{harvnb|Eisenbud|1995|loc=Theorem 10.10}}</ref>
<math display="block">\dim B/\mathfrak{m}_A B \ge \dim B - \dim A.</math>
The equality holds if <math>A \to B</math> is [[flat module|flat]] or more generally if it has the [[going-down property]].}}

Proof: Let <math>x_1, \dots, x_n</math> generate a <math>\mathfrak{m}_A</math>-primary ideal and <math>y_1, \dots, y_m</math> be such that their images generate a <math>\mathfrak{m}_B/\mathfrak{m}_A B</math>-primary ideal. Then <math>{\mathfrak{m}_B}^s \subset (y_1, \dots, y_m) + \mathfrak{m}_A B</math> for some <math>s</math>. Raising both sides to higher powers, we see some power of <math>\mathfrak{m}_B</math> is contained in <math>(y_1, \dots, y_m, x_1, \dots, x_n)</math>; i.e., the latter ideal is <math>\mathfrak{m}_B</math>-primary; thus, <math>m + n \ge \dim B</math>. The equality is a straightforward application of the going-down property. [[Q.E.D.]]

{{math_theorem|name=Proposition|If <math>R</math> is a noetherian ring, then <math display="block">\dim R + 1 = \dim R[x] = \dim R[\![x]\!].</math>}}
Proof: If <math>\mathfrak{p}_0 \subsetneq \mathfrak{p}_1 \subsetneq \cdots \subsetneq \mathfrak{p}_n</math> are a chain of prime ideals in <math>R</math>, then <math>\mathfrak{p}_iR[x]</math> are a chain of prime ideals in <math>R[x]</math> while <math>\mathfrak{p}_nR[x]</math> is not a maximal ideal. Thus, <math>\dim R + 1 \le \dim R[x]</math>. For the reverse inequality, let <math>\mathfrak{m}</math> be a maximal ideal of <math>R[x]</math> and <math>\mathfrak{p} = R \cap \mathfrak{m}</math>. Clearly, <math>R[x]_\mathfrak{m} = R_{\mathfrak{p}}[x]_\mathfrak{m}</math>.
Since <math>R[x]_{\mathfrak{m}} / \mathfrak{p} R_{\mathfrak{p}} R[x]_{\mathfrak{m}} = (R_{\mathfrak{p}}/\mathfrak{p}R_{\mathfrak{p}})[x]_{\mathfrak{m}}</math> is then a localization of a [[principal ideal domain]] and has dimension at most one, we get <math>1 + \dim R \ge 1 + \dim R_\mathfrak{p} \ge \dim R[x]_\mathfrak{m}</math> by the previous inequality. Since <math>\mathfrak{m}</math> is arbitrary, it follows <math>1 + \dim R \ge \dim R[x]</math>. Q.E.D.

=== Nagata's altitude formula ===
{{math_theorem|Let <math>R \subset R'</math> be integral domains, <math>\mathfrak{p}' \subset R'</math> be a prime ideal and <math>\mathfrak{p} = R \cap \mathfrak{p}'</math>. If <math>R</math> is a Noetherian ring, then
<math display="block">\dim R'_{\mathfrak{p}'} + \operatorname{tr.deg}_{R/\mathfrak{p}} {R'/\mathfrak{p}'} \le \dim R_{\mathfrak{p}} + \operatorname{tr.deg}_{R} {R'}</math>
where the equality holds if either (a) <math>R</math> is [[universally catenary]] and <math>R'</math> is finitely generated <math>R</math>-algebra or (b) <math>R'</math> is a polynomial ring over <math>R</math>.}}

Proof:<ref>{{harvnb|Matsumura|1987|loc=Theorem 15.5.}}</ref> First suppose <math>R'</math> is a polynomial ring. By induction on the number of variables, it is enough to consider the case <math>R' = R[x]</math>. Since <math>R'</math> is flat over <math>R</math>,
<math display="block">\dim R'_{\mathfrak{p'}} = \dim R_{\mathfrak{p}} + \dim \kappa(\mathfrak{p}) \otimes_R {R'}_{\mathfrak{p}'}.</math>
By [[Noether's normalization lemma]], the second term on the right side is:
<math display="block">\dim \kappa(\mathfrak{p}) \otimes_R R' - \dim \kappa(\mathfrak{p}) \otimes_R R'/\mathfrak{p}' = 1 - \operatorname{tr.deg}_{\kappa(\mathfrak{p})} \kappa(\mathfrak{p}') = \operatorname{tr.deg}_R R' - \operatorname{tr.deg} \kappa(\mathfrak{p}').</math>
Next, suppose <math>R'</math> is generated by a single element; thus, <math>R' = R[x]/I</math>. If <math>I</math> = 0, then we are already done. Suppose not. Then <math>R'</math> is algebraic over <math>R</math> and so <math>\operatorname{tr.deg}_R R' = 0</math>. Since <math>R</math> is a subring of <math>R'</math>, <math>I \cap R = 0</math> and so <math>\operatorname{ht} I = \dim R[x]_I = \dim Q(R)[x]_I = 1 - \operatorname{tr.deg}_{Q(R)} \kappa(I) = 1</math>
since <math>\kappa(I) = Q(R')</math> is algebraic over <math>Q(R)</math>. Let <math>\mathfrak{p}^{\prime c}</math> denote the pre-image in <math>R[x]</math> of <math>\mathfrak{p}'</math>. Then, as <math>\kappa(\mathfrak{p}^{\prime c}) = \kappa(\mathfrak{p})</math>, by the polynomial case,
<math display="block">\operatorname{ht}{\mathfrak{p}'} = \operatorname{ht}{\mathfrak{p}^{\prime c}/I} \le \operatorname{ht}{\mathfrak{p}^{\prime c}} - \operatorname{ht}{I} = \dim R_{\mathfrak{p}} - \operatorname{tr.deg}_{\kappa(\mathfrak{p})} \kappa(\mathfrak{p}').</math>
Here, note that the inequality is the equality if <math>R'</math> is catenary. Finally, working with a chain of prime ideals, it is straightforward to reduce the general case to the above case. Q.E.D.

{{See also|Quasi-unmixed ring}}

== Homological methods ==

=== Regular rings ===
Let <math>R</math> be a noetherian ring. The [[projective dimension]] of a finite <math>R</math>-module <math>M</math> is the shortest length of any [[projective resolution]] of <math>M</math> (possibly infinite) and is denoted by <math>\operatorname{pd}_R M</math>. We set <math>\operatorname{gl.dim} R = \sup \{ \operatorname{pd}_R M \mid M\text{ is a finite module} \}</math>; it is called the [[global dimension]] of <math>R</math>.

Assume <math>R</math> is local with residue field <math>k</math>.

{{math_theorem|name=Lemma|<math>\operatorname{pd}_R k = \operatorname{gl.dim} R</math> (possibly infinite).}}

Proof: We claim: for any finite <math>R</math>-module <math>M</math>,
<math display="block">\operatorname{pd}_R M \le n \Leftrightarrow \operatorname{Tor}^R_{n+1}(M, k) = 0.</math>
By dimension shifting (cf. the proof of Theorem of Serre below), it is enough to prove this for <math>n = 0</math>. But then, by the [[local criterion for flatness]], <math>\operatorname{Tor}^R_1(M, k) = 0 \Rightarrow M\text{ flat } \Rightarrow M\text{ free } \Rightarrow \operatorname{pd}_R(M) \le 0.</math>
Now,
<math display="block">\operatorname{gl.dim} R \le n \Rightarrow \operatorname{pd}_R k \le n \Rightarrow \operatorname{Tor}^R_{n+1}(-, k) = 0 \Rightarrow \operatorname{pd}_R - \le n \Rightarrow \operatorname{gl.dim} R \le n,</math>
completing the proof. Q.E.D.

'''Remark''': The proof also shows that <math>\operatorname{pd}_R K = \operatorname{pd}_R M - 1</math> if <math>M</math> is not free and <math>K</math> is the kernel of some surjection from a [[free module]] to <math>M</math>.

{{math_theorem|name=Lemma|Let <math>R_1 = R/fR</math>, <math>f</math> a non-zerodivisor of <math>R</math>. If <math>f</math> is a non-zerodivisor on <math>M</math>, then <math display="block">\operatorname{pd}_R M \ge \operatorname{pd}_{R_1} (M \otimes R_1).</math>}}

Proof: If <math>\operatorname{pd}_R M = 0</math>, then <math>M</math> is <math>R</math>-free and thus <math>M \otimes R_1</math> is <math>R_1</math>-free. Next suppose <math>\operatorname{pd}_R M > 0</math>. Then we have: <math>\operatorname{pd}_R K = \operatorname{pd}_R M - 1</math> as in the remark above. Thus, by induction, it is enough to consider the case <math>\operatorname{pd}_R M = 1</math>. Then there is a projective resolution: <math>0 \to P_1 \to P_0 \to M \to 0</math>, which gives:
<math display="block">\operatorname{Tor}^R_1(M, R_1) \to P_1 \otimes R_1 \to P_0 \otimes R_1 \to M \otimes R_1 \to 0.</math>
But <math>\operatorname{Tor}^R_1(M, R_1) = {}_f M = \{ m \in M \mid fm = 0 \} = 0.</math> Hence, <math>\operatorname{pd}_R (M \otimes R_1)</math> is at most 1. Q.E.D.

{{math_theorem|name=Theorem of Serre|<math>R</math> regular <math>\Leftrightarrow \operatorname{gl.dim}R < \infty \Leftrightarrow \operatorname{gl.dim}R = \dim R.</math>}}

Proof:<ref>{{harvnb|Weibel|1995|loc=Theorem 4.4.16}}</ref> If <math>R</math> is regular, we can write <math>k = R/(f_1, \dots, f_n)</math>, <math>f_i</math> a regular system of parameters. An exact sequence <math>0 \to M \overset{f}\to M \to M_1 \to 0</math>, some <math>f</math> in the maximal ideal, of finite modules, <math>\operatorname{pd}_R M < \infty</math>, gives us:
<math display="block">0 = \operatorname{Tor}^R_{i+1}(M, k) \to \operatorname{Tor}^R_{i+1}(M_1, k) \to \operatorname{Tor}^R_i(M, k) \overset{f}\to \operatorname{Tor}^R_i(M, k), \quad i \ge \operatorname{pd}_R M.</math>
But <math>f</math> here is zero since it kills <math>k</math>. Thus, <math>\operatorname{Tor}^R_{i+1}(M_1, k) \simeq \operatorname{Tor}^R_i(M, k)</math> and consequently <math>\operatorname{pd}_R M_1 = 1 + \operatorname{pd}_R M</math>. Using this, we get:
<math display="block">\operatorname{pd}_R k = 1 + \operatorname{pd}_R (R/(f_1, \dots, f_{n-1})) = \cdots = n.</math>
The proof of the converse is by induction on <math>\dim R</math>. We begin with the inductive step. Set <math>R_1 = R/f_1 R</math>, <math>f_1</math> among a system of parameters. To show <math>R</math> is regular, it is enough to show <math>R_1</math> is regular. But, since <math>\dim R_1 < \dim R</math>, by inductive hypothesis and the preceding lemma with <math>M = \mathfrak{m}</math>,
<math display="block">\operatorname{gl.dim} R < \infty \Rightarrow \operatorname{gl.dim} R_1 = \operatorname{pd}_{R_1} k \le \operatorname{pd}_{R_1} \mathfrak{m} / f_1 \mathfrak{m} < \infty \Rightarrow R_1 \text{ regular}.</math>

The basic step remains. Suppose <math>\dim R = 0</math>. We claim <math>\operatorname{gl.dim}R = 0</math> if it is finite. (This would imply that <math>R</math> is a [[semisimple local ring]]; i.e., a field.) If that is not the case, then there is some finite module <math>M</math> with <math>0 < \operatorname{pd}_R M < \infty</math> and thus in fact we can find <math>M</math> with <math>\operatorname{pd}_R M = 1</math>. By [[Nakayama's lemma]], there is a surjection <math>F \to M</math> from a free module <math>F</math> to <math>M</math> whose kernel <math>K</math> is contained in <math>\mathfrak{m} F</math>. Since <math>\dim R = 0</math>, the maximal ideal <math>\mathfrak{m}</math> is an [[associated prime]] of <math>R</math>; i.e., <math>\mathfrak{m} = \operatorname{ann}(s)</math> for some nonzero <math>s</math> in <math>R</math>. Since <math>K \subset \mathfrak{m} F</math>, <math>s K = 0</math>. Since <math>K</math> is not zero and is free, this implies <math>s = 0</math>, which is absurd. Q.E.D.

{{math_theorem|name=Corollary|A regular local ring is a unique factorization domain.}}

Proof: Let <math>R</math> be a regular local ring. Then <math>\operatorname{gr}R \simeq k[x_1, \dots, x_d]</math>, which is an [[integrally closed domain]]. It is a standard algebra exercise to show this implies that <math>R</math> is an integrally closed domain. Now, we need to show every [[divisorial ideal]] is principal; i.e., the divisor class group of <math>R</math> vanishes. But, according to Bourbaki, ''Algèbre commutative,'' chapitre 7, §. 4. Corollary 2 to Proposition 16, a divisorial ideal is principal if it admits a finite free resolution, which is indeed the case by the theorem. Q.E.D.

{{math_theorem|Let <math>R</math> be a ring. Then <math display="block">\operatorname{gl.dim} R[x_1, \dots, x_n] = \operatorname{gl.dim} R + n.</math>}}

=== Depth ===

Let <math>R</math> be a ring and <math>M</math> a module over it. A sequence of elements <math>x_1, \dots, x_n</math> in <math>R</math> is called an <math>M</math>-[[regular sequence]] if <math>x_1</math> is not a zero-divisor on <math>M</math> and <math>x_i</math> is not a [[zero divisor]] on <math>M/(x_1, \dots, x_{i-1})M</math> for each <math>i = 2, \dots, n</math>. ''A priori'', it is not obvious whether any permutation of a regular sequence is still regular (see the section below for some positive answer).

Let <math>R</math> be a local Noetherian ring with maximal ideal <math>\mathfrak{m}</math> and put <math>k = R/\mathfrak{m}</math>. Then, by definition, the [[depth (ring theory)|depth]] of a finite <math>R</math>-module <math>M</math> is the supremum of the lengths of all <math>M</math>-regular sequences in <math>\mathfrak{m}</math>. For example, we have <math>\operatorname{depth} M = 0 \Leftrightarrow \mathfrak{m}</math> consists of zerodivisors on <math>M</math> <math>\Leftrightarrow \mathfrak{m}</math> is associated with <math>M</math>. By induction, we find
<math display="block">\operatorname{depth} M \le \dim R/{\mathfrak{p}}</math>
for any associated primes <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> of <math>M</math>. In particular, <math>\operatorname{depth} M \le \dim M</math>. If the equality holds for <math>M</math> = <math>R</math>, <math>R</math> is called a [[Cohen–Macaulay ring]].

'''Example''': A regular Noetherian local ring is Cohen–Macaulay (since a regular system of parameters is an <math>R</math>-regular sequence).

In general, a Noetherian ring is called a Cohen–Macaulay ring if the localizations at all maximal ideals are Cohen–Macaulay. We note that a Cohen–Macaulay ring is universally catenary. This implies for example that a polynomial ring <math>k[x_1, \dots, x_d]</math> is universally catenary since it is regular and thus Cohen–Macaulay.

{{math_theorem|name=Proposition|note=Rees|Let <math>M</math> be a finite <math>R</math>-module. Then the [[Ext functor]] satisfies <math>\operatorname{depth} M = \sup \{ n \mid \operatorname{Ext}_R^i(k, M) = 0, i < n \}</math>.

More generally, for any finite <math>R</math>-module <math>N</math> whose [[Support of a module|support]] is exactly <math>\{ \mathfrak{m} \}</math>,
<math display="block">\operatorname{depth} M = \sup \{ n \mid \operatorname{Ext}_R^i(N, M) = 0, i < n \}.</math>}}

Proof: We first prove by induction on <math>n</math> the following statement: for every <math>R</math>-module <math>M</math> and every <math>M</math>-regular sequence <math>x_1, \dots, x_n</math> in <math>\mathfrak{m}</math>,
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\operatorname{Ext}_R^n(N, M) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_R(N, M/(x_1, \dots, x_n) M).</math>|{{EquationRef|⁎}}}}
The basic step <math>n</math> = 0 is trivial. Next, by inductive hypothesis, <math>\operatorname{Ext}_R^{n-1}(N, M) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_R(N, M/(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}) M)</math>. But the latter is zero since the annihilator of <math>N</math> contains some power of <math>x_n</math>. Thus, from the exact sequence <math>0 \to M \overset{x_1} \to M \to M_1 \to 0</math> and the fact that <math>x_1</math> kills <math>N</math>, using the inductive hypothesis again, we get
<math display="block">\operatorname{Ext}^n_R(N, M) \simeq \operatorname{Ext}^{n-1}_R(N, M/x_1 M) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_R(N, M/(x_1, \dots, x_n) M),</math>
proving ({{EquationNote|⁎}}). Now, if <math>n < \operatorname{depth} M</math>, then we can find an <math>M</math>-regular sequence of length more than <math>n</math> and so by ({{EquationNote|⁎}}) we see <math>\operatorname{Ext}_R^n(N, M) = 0</math>. It remains to show <math>\operatorname{Ext}_R^n(N, M) \ne 0</math> if <math>n = \operatorname{depth} M</math>. By ({{EquationNote|⁎}}) we can assume <math>n</math> = 0. Then <math>\mathfrak{m}</math> is associated with <math>M</math>; thus is in the support of <math>M</math>. On the other hand, <math>\mathfrak{m} \in \operatorname{Supp}(N).</math> It follows by linear algebra that there is a nonzero homomorphism from <math>N</math> to <math>M</math> modulo <math>\mathfrak{m}</math>; hence, one from <math>N</math> to <math>M</math> by Nakayama's lemma. Q.E.D.

The [[Auslander–Buchsbaum formula]] relates depth and projective dimension.

{{math_theorem|Let <math>M</math> be a finite module over a noetherian local ring <math>R</math>. If <math>\operatorname{pd}_R M < \infty</math>, then <math display="block">\operatorname{pd}_R M + \operatorname{depth} M = \operatorname{depth} R.</math>}}
Proof: We argue by induction on <math>\operatorname{pd}_R M</math>, the basic case (i.e., <math>M</math> free) being trivial. By Nakayama's lemma, we have the exact sequence <math>0 \to K \overset{f}\to F \to M \to 0</math> where <math>F</math> is free and the image of <math>f</math> is contained in <math>\mathfrak{m} F</math>. Since <math>\operatorname{pd}_R K = \operatorname{pd}_R M - 1,</math> what we need to show is <math>\operatorname{depth} K = \operatorname{depth} M + 1</math>.
Since <math>f</math> kills <math>k</math>, the [[exact sequence]] yields: for any <math>i</math>,
<math display="block">\operatorname{Ext}_R^i(k, F) \to \operatorname{Ext}_R^i(k, M) \to \operatorname{Ext}_R^{i+1}(k, K) \to 0.</math>
Note the left-most term is zero if <math>i < \operatorname{depth} R</math>. If <math>i < \operatorname{depth} K - 1</math>, then since <math>\operatorname{depth} K \le \operatorname{depth} R</math> by inductive hypothesis, we see <math>\operatorname{Ext}_R^i(k, M) = 0.</math> If <math>i = \operatorname{depth} K - 1</math>, then <math>\operatorname{Ext}_R^{i+1}(k, K) \ne 0</math> and it must be <math>\operatorname{Ext}_R^i(k, M) \ne 0.</math> Q.E.D.

As a matter of notation, for any <math>R</math>-module <math>M</math>, we let
<math display="block">\Gamma_{\mathfrak{m}}(M) = \{ s \in M \mid \operatorname{supp}(s) \subset \{ \mathfrak{m} \} \} = \{ s \in M \mid \mathfrak{m}^j s = 0 \text{ for some } j \}.</math>
One sees without difficulty that <math>\Gamma_{\mathfrak{m}}</math> is a [[left-exact functor]] and then let <math>H^j_{\mathfrak{m}} = R^j \Gamma_{\mathfrak{m}}</math> be its <math>j</math>-th [[right derived functor]], called the [[local cohomology]] of <math>R</math>. Since <math>\Gamma_{\mathfrak{m}}(M) = \varinjlim \operatorname{Hom}_R(R/\mathfrak{m}^j, M)</math>, via abstract nonsense,
<math display="block">H^i_{\mathfrak{m}}(M) = \varinjlim \operatorname{Ext}^i_R (R/{\mathfrak{m}}^j, M).</math>
This observation proves the first part of the theorem below.
{{math_theorem|note=Grothendieck|Let <math>M</math> be a finite <math>R</math>-module. Then
# <math>\operatorname{depth} \operatorname{M} = \sup \{ n \mid H^i_{\mathfrak{m}}(M) = 0, i < n \}</math>.
# <math>H_{\mathfrak{m} }^i(M) = 0, i > \dim M</math> and <math>\ne 0</math> if <math>i = \dim M.</math><!-- (TODO: this part apparently needs [[Koszul complex]].)-->
# If <math>R</math> is complete and <math>d</math> its Krull dimension and if <math>E</math> is the [[injective hull]] of <math>k</math>, then <math display="block">\operatorname{Hom}_R(H^d_{ \mathfrak{m} }(-), E)</math> is representable (the representing object is sometimes called the [[canonical module]] especially if <math>R</math> is Cohen–Macaulay).
}}
Proof: 1. is already noted (except to show the nonvanishing at the degree equal to the depth of <math>M</math>; use induction to see this) and 3. is a general fact by abstract nonsense. 2. is a consequence of an explicit computation of a local cohomology by means of Koszul complexes (see below). <math>\square</math>

=== Koszul complex ===
{{main|Koszul complex}}

Let <math>R</math> be a ring and <math>x</math> an element in it. We form the [[chain complex]] <math>K</math>(<math>x</math>) given by <math>K(x)_i = R</math> for <math>i</math> = 0, 1 and <math>K(x)_i = 0</math> for any other <math>i</math> with the differential
<math display="block">d: K_1(R) \to K_0(R), \, r \mapsto xr.</math>
For any <math>R</math>-module <math>M</math>, we then get the complex <math>K(x, M) = K(x) \otimes_R M</math> with the differential <math>d \otimes 1</math> and let <math>\operatorname{H}_*(x, M) = \operatorname{H}_*(K(x, M))</math> be its homology. Note:
<math display="block">\operatorname{H}_0(x, M) = M/xM ,</math>
<math display="block">\operatorname{H}_1(x, M) = {}_x M = \{ m \in M \mid xm = 0 \}.</math>

More generally, given a finite sequence <math>x_1, \dots, x_n</math> of elements in a ring <math>R</math>, we form the [[tensor product of complexes]]:
<math display="block">K(x_1, \dots, x_n) = K(x_1) \otimes \dots \otimes K(x_n)</math>
and let <math>\operatorname{H}_*(x_1, \dots, x_n, M) = \operatorname{H}_*(K(x_1, \dots, x_n, M))</math> its homology. As before,
<math display="block">\operatorname{H}_0(\underline{x}, M) = M/(x_1, \dots, x_n)M,</math>
<math display="block">\operatorname{H}_n(\underline{x}, M) = \operatorname{Ann}_M((x_1, \dots, x_n)).</math>

We now have the homological characterization of a regular sequence.
{{math_theorem|name=Theorem|Suppose <math>R</math> is Noetherian, <math>M</math> is a finite module over <math>R</math> and <math>x_i</math> are in the [[Jacobson radical]] of <math>R</math>. Then the following are equivalent
{{ordered list|list-style-type=lower-roman
|1=<math>\underline{x}</math> is an <math>M</math>-regular sequence.
|2=<math>\operatorname{H}_i(\underline{x}, M) = 0, i \ge 1</math>.
|3=<math>\operatorname{H}_1(\underline{x}, M) = 0</math>.}}}}

{{math_theorem|name=Corollary|The sequence <math>x_i</math> is <math>M</math>-regular if and only if any of its permutations is so.}}

{{math_theorem|name=Corollary|If <math>x_1, \dots, x_n</math> is an <math>M</math>-regular sequence, then <math>x_1^j, \dots, x_n^j</math> is also an <math>M</math>-regular sequence for each positive integer <math>j</math>.}}

A Koszul complex is a powerful computational tool. For instance, it follows from the theorem and the corollary
<math display="block">\operatorname{H}^i_{\mathfrak{m}}(M) \simeq \varinjlim \operatorname{H}^i(K(x_1^j, \dots, x_n^j; M))</math>
(Here, one uses the self-duality of a Koszul complex; see Proposition 17.15. of Eisenbud, ''Commutative Algebra with a View Toward Algebraic Geometry''.)

Another instance would be
{{math_theorem|Assume <math>R</math> is local. Then let
<math display="block">s = \dim_k \mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2,</math>
the dimension of the [[Zariski tangent space]] (often called the [[embedding dimension]] of <math>R</math>). Then
<math display="block">\binom{s}{i} \le \dim_k \operatorname{Tor}^R_i(k, k).</math>}}

'''Remark''': The theorem can be used to give a second quick proof of Serre's theorem, that <math>R</math> is regular [[if and only if]] it has finite global dimension. Indeed, by the above theorem, <math>\operatorname{Tor}^R_s(k, k) \ne 0</math> and thus <math>\operatorname{gl.dim} R \ge s</math>. On the other hand, as <math>\operatorname{gl.dim} R = \operatorname{pd}_R k</math>, the Auslander–Buchsbaum formula gives <math>\operatorname{gl.dim} R = \dim R</math>. Hence, <math>\dim R \le s \le \operatorname{gl.dim} R = \dim R</math>.

We next use a Koszul homology to define and study [[complete intersection ring]]s. Let <math>R</math> be a Noetherian local ring. By definition, the [[first deviation]] of <math>R</math> is the vector space dimension
<math display="block">\epsilon_1(R) = \dim_k \operatorname{H}_1(\underline{x})</math>
where <math>\underline{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_d)</math> is a system of parameters. By definition, <math>R</math> is a complete intersection ring if <math>\dim R + \epsilon_1(R)</math> is the dimension of the tangent space. (See Hartshorne for a geometric meaning.)

{{math_theorem|<math>R</math> is a complete intersection ring if and only if its Koszul algebra is an [[exterior algebra]].}}

=== Injective dimension and Tor dimensions ===
Let <math>R</math> be a ring. The [[injective dimension]] of an <math>R</math>-module <math>M</math> denoted by <math>\operatorname{id}_R M</math> is defined just like a projective dimension: it is the minimal length of an injective resolution of <math>M</math>. Let <math>\operatorname{Mod}_R</math> be the category of <math>R</math>-modules.

{{math_theorem|For any ring <math>R</math>,
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\operatorname{gl.dim} R \, &= \operatorname{sup} \{ \operatorname{id}_R M \mid M \in \operatorname{Mod}_R \} \\
&= \inf \{ n \mid \operatorname{Ext}^i_R(M, N) = 0, \, i > n, M, N \in \operatorname{Mod}_R \}
\end{align}</math>}}

Proof: Suppose <math>\operatorname{gl.dim} R \le n</math>. Let <math>M</math> be an <math>R</math>-module and consider a resolution
<math display="block">0 \to M \to I_0 \overset{\phi_0}\to I_1 \to \dots \to I_{n-1} \overset{\phi_{n-1}}\to N \to 0</math>
where <math>I_i</math> are injective modules. For any ideal <math>I</math>,
<math display="block">\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(R/I, N) \simeq \operatorname{Ext}^2_R(R/I, \operatorname{ker}(\phi_{n-1})) \simeq \dots \simeq \operatorname{Ext}_R^{n+1}(R/I, M),</math>
which is zero since <math>\operatorname{Ext}_R^{n+1}(R/I, -)</math> is computed via a projective resolution of <math>R/I</math>. Thus, by [[Baer's criterion]], <math>N</math> is injective. We conclude that <math>\sup \{ \operatorname{id}_R M | M \} \le n</math>. Essentially by reversing the arrows, one can also prove the implication in the other way. Q.E.D.

The theorem suggests that we consider a sort of a dual of a global dimension:
<math display="block">\operatorname{w.gl.dim} = \inf \{ n \mid \operatorname{Tor}^R_i(M, N) = 0, \, i > n, M, N \in \operatorname{Mod}_R \} .</math>
It was originally called the weak global dimension of <math>R</math> but today it is more commonly called the [[Tor dimension]] of <math>R</math>.

'''Remark:''' for any ring <math>R</math>, <math>\operatorname{w.gl.dim} R \le \operatorname{gl.dim} R</math>.

{{math_theorem|name=Proposition|A ring has weak global dimension zero if and only if it is [[von Neumann regular]].}}

== Dimensions of non-commutative rings ==
{{expand section|date=May 2015}}

Let <math>A</math> be a graded algebra over a field <math>k</math>. If <math>V</math> is a finite-dimensional generating subspace of <math>A</math>, then we let <math>f(n) = \dim_k V^n</math> and then put
<math display="block">\operatorname{gk}(A) = \limsup_{n \to \infty} {\log f(n) \over \log n}.</math>
It is called the [[Gelfand–Kirillov dimension]] of <math>A</math>. It is easy to show <math>\operatorname{gk}(A)</math> is independent of a choice of <math>V</math>. Given a graded right (or left) module <math>M</math> over <math>A</math> one may similarly define the Gelfand-Kirillov dimension <math>{gk}(M)</math> of <math>M</math>. 

'''Example''': If <math>A</math> is finite-dimensional, then gk(<math>A</math>) = 0. If <math>A</math> is an affine ring, then gk(<math>A</math>) = Krull dimension of <math>A</math>.<!--'''Example''': If <math>A</math> is the [[ring of differential operators]] on a smooth algebraic variety, then -->

'''Example''': If <math>A_n = k[x_1, ..., x_n, \partial_1, ..., \partial_n]</math> is the n-th [[Weyl algebra]] then <math> \operatorname{gk}(A_n) = 2n.</math>
